title: Analyze a real public dataset
goal: Produce a traceable descriptive analysis with justified exclusions and visible denominators.
prerequisites: You can clean, group, plot, and export data; review the public-data README and field dictionary.

cells.title: Check the source and audit missingness
cells.explanation: Begin a public-data analysis by identifying the source, version, and field definitions. A checksum can confirm that the local source file matches the recorded bytes, while a missingness audit tells you what is available to analyze. These checks do not prove that every scientific measurement is correct.
cells.code:
import hashlib
folder = DATA_DIR / "public"
metadata = json.loads((folder / "provenance.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
digest = hashlib.sha256((folder / "penguins.csv").read_bytes()).hexdigest()
assert digest == metadata["artifacts"]["penguins.csv"]["sha256"]
df = pd.read_csv(folder / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
result = pd.DataFrame({"Missing": df.isna().sum(), "Known": df.notna().sum()})
print("Dataset:", metadata["dataset"])
print("Source commit:", metadata["upstream"]["commit"])
print("Shape:", df.shape)
print(result)

questions.prompt: What does the checksum comparison establish?
questions.answer: The local file has the exact bytes recorded in the provenance manifest, assuming the manifest itself is trusted.

questions.prompt: Which field has more missing values: sex or body_mass_g?
questions.answer: sex has 11 missing entries, compared with two missing body masses.

questions.prompt: Why does file identity not prove scientific validity?
questions.answer: A file can be an exact copy and still contain measurement limitations, sampling constraints, or source errors.

cells.task: Read the source into df. Store a dictionary named result with keys total_rows, rows_with_any_missing, complete_rows, and rows_with_known_mass. Calculate those four counts across the source fields without deleting rows from df.
cells.hint: Use isna().any(axis=1), dropna() only for counting, and body_mass_g.notna().sum().
cells.solution:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
result = {
    "total_rows": len(df),
    "rows_with_any_missing": int(df.isna().any(axis=1).sum()),
    "complete_rows": len(df.dropna()),
    "rows_with_known_mass": int(df["body_mass_g"].notna().sum()),
}
print(result)
print("The original DataFrame still has", len(df), "rows.")
cells.solution_note: There are 344 rows, 11 with at least one missing field, 333 complete rows, and 342 with known body mass. Complete-case filtering would discard nine additional known body masses because another field is missing.

check.prompt: Which statement is justified by a matching recorded checksum?
options: The local source bytes match the recorded file
check.feedback: A checksum establishes file identity, not representativeness or correctness of the study design.

cells.verify:
assert df.shape == (344, 8)
assert result.loc["sex", "Missing"] == 11
assert result.loc["body_mass_g", "Known"] == 342
assert digest == metadata["artifacts"]["penguins.csv"]["sha256"]
cells.watch: A row position is a way to trace the source file, not an animal identifier.
cells.takeaway: Document source identity and data availability before reporting results.

cells.title: Choose exclusions to match the question
cells.explanation: A body-mass summary needs a known body mass and a grouping label. It does not automatically need recorded sex. Keep an exclusion audit and retain original units; this exercise does not replace missing measurements with invented values.
cells.code:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
df.insert(0, "source_row", np.arange(1, len(df) + 1))
required = ["species", "body_mass_g"]
missing_required = df[required].isna().any(axis=1)
audit = df.loc[missing_required, ["source_row"] + required].copy()
result = df.loc[~missing_required].copy()
assert result["body_mass_g"].gt(0).all()
print("Rows retained:", len(result))
print("Excluded rows:")
print(audit)
print("Retained rows with unrecorded sex:", result["sex"].isna().sum())

questions.prompt: Which two fields control inclusion in this cell?
Will every retained row also have a recorded sex?
questions.answer: No. Nine retained rows have a known mass but missing sex.

questions.prompt: Why is source_row useful, and what does it not establish?
questions.answer: It traces a record to its one-based position in the source table. It is not a biological identity or a repeated-measurement ID.

cells.task: Change the question to body-mass summaries by species and sex. Require species, sex, and body_mass_g. Recreate the retained result and exclusion audit from the original file; do not reuse the earlier filtered table.
cells.hint: Add sex to required and rebuild the missing-required mask.
cells.solution:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
df.insert(0, "source_row", np.arange(1, len(df) + 1))
required = ["species", "sex", "body_mass_g"]
missing_required = df[required].isna().any(axis=1)
audit = df.loc[missing_required, ["source_row"] + required].copy()
result = df.loc[~missing_required].copy()
print("Rows retained:", len(result))
print("Rows excluded:", len(audit))
print(audit)
cells.solution_note: The revised question retains 333 records and excludes 11. The decision changed because the requested grouping now needs sex; it is not a rule that every analysis must use complete cases.

check.prompt: Why keep some rows with missing sex for the original mass-by-species question?
options: Sex is not required for that stated summary
Missing sex is equivalent to male
check.feedback: A required-field policy should match the analysis question and still report what is missing.

cells.verify:
assert len(result) == 342
assert len(audit) == 2
assert result["sex"].isna().sum() == 9
assert result["body_mass_g"].notna().all()
assert len(result) + len(audit) == 344
cells.solution_verify:
assert len(result) == 333
assert len(audit) == 11
assert result[["species", "sex", "body_mass_g"]].notna().all().all()
assert len(result) + len(audit) == 344
cells.watch: Report exclusions and consider whether the remaining observations differ systematically; these checks do not establish random missingness.
cells.takeaway: Define the required fields and preserve an exclusion audit.

cells.title: Report group means with their denominators
cells.explanation: A group mean uses the known measurements in that group. Show total observations, known measurements, and missing measurements beside the mean so readers can see its denominator. The summaries describe these observations; they do not establish causal species or island effects.
cells.code:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
result = df.groupby("species", as_index=False).agg(Observations=("species", "size"), Known_mass=("body_mass_g", "count"), Mean_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"))
result["Missing_mass"] = result["Observations"] - result["Known_mass"]
print(result.round({"Mean_mass_g": 2}))
print("Total observed records:", result["Observations"].sum())
print("Total known body masses:", result["Known_mass"].sum())

questions.prompt: What is the denominator for the Adelie mean mass?
questions.answer: 151 known body masses, not all 152 Adelie observations.

questions.prompt: Which species has no missing body masses in this table?
questions.answer: Chinstrap: all 68 observations have known body mass.

questions.prompt: Can these group means alone explain why the species differ in body mass?
questions.answer: No. They are descriptive summaries; causal explanations require an appropriate design and relevant evidence.

cells.task: Group by island instead of species. Store result with island as a normal column, sorted in ascending island order, and report Observations, Known_mass, Missing_mass, and Mean_mass_g. Reconcile the total observations and known measurements with the full table.
cells.hint: Change the grouping key and keep the matching size/count denominators.
cells.solution:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
result = df.groupby("island", as_index=False).agg(Observations=("island", "size"), Known_mass=("body_mass_g", "count"), Mean_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"))
result["Missing_mass"] = result["Observations"] - result["Known_mass"]
assert result["Observations"].sum() == len(df)
assert result["Known_mass"].sum() == df["body_mass_g"].count()
print(result.round({"Mean_mass_g": 2}))
cells.solution_note: Biscoe has 168 observations and 167 known masses; Dream has 124 and 124; Torgersen has 52 and 51. Their mean masses are approximately 4,716.02 g, 3,712.90 g, and 3,706.37 g. Different species composition is one reason to avoid interpreting these as an isolated island effect.

check.prompt: What should accompany a mean when values are missing?
options: The number of known measurements used
A claim that missing values are zero
check.feedback: The known-value count tells the reader what supports the mean.

cells.verify:
assert result["Observations"].sum() == 344
assert result["Known_mass"].sum() == 342
assert result["Missing_mass"].tolist() == [1, 0, 1]
assert result.set_index("species").loc["Adelie", "Known_mass"] == 151
assert np.isclose(result.set_index("species").loc["Gentoo", "Mean_mass_g"], 624350 / 123)
cells.solution_verify:
assert result["Observations"].tolist() == [168, 124, 52]
assert result["Known_mass"].tolist() == [167, 124, 51]
assert result["Missing_mass"].sum() == 2
assert np.isclose(result.set_index("island").loc["Dream", "Mean_mass_g"], 460400 / 124)
cells.watch: Sample sizes and species composition differ across islands. A descriptive comparison is not an adjusted causal analysis.
cells.takeaway: Pair every summary with its relevant count and interpretation.

cells.title: Create a chart and an auditable export
cells.explanation: Combine the source, missingness policy, grouped summary, chart, and export into one repeatable cell. Keep counts in the exported table and label the plotted units. A chart can summarize the sampled measurements without claiming a population estimate or a causal finding.
cells.code:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
result = df.groupby("species", as_index=False).agg(Observations=("species", "size"), Known_mass=("body_mass_g", "count"), Mean_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"))
result["Missing_mass"] = result["Observations"] - result["Known_mass"]
result["Mean_mass_kg"] = result["Mean_mass_g"] / 1000
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.bar(result["species"], result["Mean_mass_kg"], color="#326f79")
for i, row in result.iterrows():
    ax.text(i, row["Mean_mass_kg"] + 0.08, f"n={int(row['Known_mass'])}", ha="center")
ax.set(title="Mean observed penguin body mass, 2007–2009", xlabel="Species", ylabel="Mean body mass (kg)", ylim=(0, 6))
fig.tight_layout()
csv_path = OUTPUT_DIR / "public_penguins_mass_summary.csv"
plot_path = OUTPUT_DIR / "public_penguins_mass_summary.png"
result.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)
fig.savefig(plot_path, dpi=160)
print(result.round({"Mean_mass_g": 2, "Mean_mass_kg": 3}))
print("Source: Palmer Penguins; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3960218. Means use known body masses.")
print("These summaries describe sampled observations, not causal effects or a population census.")
plt.show()

questions.prompt: What does each n label above a bar count?
questions.answer: The known body masses used to calculate that species mean.

questions.prompt: Will converting grams to kilograms change which species has the largest mean in this table?
questions.answer: No. Every mean is divided by the same positive factor of 1,000.

questions.prompt: Why export the counts and missing counts as well as the plotted mean?
questions.answer: They preserve the analysis denominator and make it easier to audit how the result was calculated.

cells.task: Build result as a summary by species in ascending species order, with columns species, Observations, Known_length, Median_flipper_mm, and Missing_length. Plot the medians with known-count labels on axes named ax, using the y-axis label "Median flipper length (mm)". Set csv_path and plot_path to public_penguins_flipper_summary.csv and public_penguins_flipper_summary.png in OUTPUT_DIR, then export the table and chart.
cells.hint: Change the measurement, summary method, labels, and filenames together; do not reuse the mass units.
cells.solution:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "public" / "penguins.csv", na_values=["NA"])
result = df.groupby("species", as_index=False).agg(Observations=("species", "size"), Known_length=("flipper_length_mm", "count"), Median_flipper_mm=("flipper_length_mm", "median"))
result["Missing_length"] = result["Observations"] - result["Known_length"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.bar(result["species"], result["Median_flipper_mm"], color="#326f79")
for i, row in result.iterrows():
    ax.text(i, row["Median_flipper_mm"] + 3, f"n={int(row['Known_length'])}", ha="center")
ax.set(title="Median observed penguin flipper length, 2007–2009", xlabel="Species", ylabel="Median flipper length (mm)", ylim=(0, 250))
fig.tight_layout()
csv_path = OUTPUT_DIR / "public_penguins_flipper_summary.csv"
plot_path = OUTPUT_DIR / "public_penguins_flipper_summary.png"
result.to_csv(csv_path, index=False)
fig.savefig(plot_path, dpi=160)
print(result)
print("Source: Palmer Penguins; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3960218. Medians use known lengths.")
print("The chart describes the available study observations; it is not a causal analysis.")
plt.show()
cells.solution_note: The median flipper lengths are 190 mm for Adelie, 196 mm for Chinstrap, and 216 mm for Gentoo, based on 151, 68, and 123 known measurements. The table and chart use the same units and denominators.

check.prompt: Which label correctly describes the plotted output?
options: The true body mass of every penguin worldwide
Mean observed body mass in the supplied study records
Proof that island location causes body mass
check.feedback: The chart summarizes the available observations with their measurement counts.

cells.verify:
assert result["Observations"].sum() == 344
assert result["Known_mass"].sum() == 342
assert result["Missing_mass"].sum() == 2
assert csv_path.exists() and plot_path.exists()
assert ax.get_ylabel() == "Mean body mass (kg)"
assert ax.get_ylim()[0] == 0
assert len(pd.read_csv(csv_path)) == 3
cells.solution_verify:
assert result["Median_flipper_mm"].tolist() == [190.0, 196.0, 216.0]
assert result["Known_length"].tolist() == [151, 68, 123]
assert result["Missing_length"].sum() == 2
assert csv_path.exists() and plot_path.exists()
assert ax.get_ylabel() == "Median flipper length (mm)"
assert len(pd.read_csv(csv_path)) == 3
cells.watch: Do not imply uncertainty intervals or representativeness that the chart has not calculated or established.
cells.takeaway: Deliver the result with its source, units, counts, and limits.
